items.title: ESA targets Anbernic emulation handhelds as "superfake" piracy enablers
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.content: For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of "Notorious Markets" that "engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting." TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more—notes that Anbernic devices "are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members." While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through "normal retail channels" help to "normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product." This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a "superfake," an ill-defined designation that applies to "high-quality counterfeit trademark goods ... on a commercial scale." Read full article Comments

items.title: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
items.content: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month! This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube. Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2, a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude. They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1, that has to be seen to be believed: In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy, and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack. From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers. We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason’s journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna. We discuss: Why Dyna-2 was trained on over one million hours of human video World-action models: predicting future video to guide physical robot actions Diffusion transformers, flow matching, and real-time robotic control How robots learn new tasks with as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations Why robotics has no equivalent of the internet and data remains its biggest scaling challenge Human egocentric video, robot demonstrations, and cross-embodiment transfer Synthetic environments, simulation, and models that generate their own training data Why robots need on-device inference, model distillation, and custom hardware Why Dyna chose wheeled semi-humanoids instead of traditional bipedal robots The hardware bottleneck: why dexterous robot hands still overheat Best Western, Din Tai Fung, and the difference between robotics pilots and scaled deployments The Bitter Lesson of Robotics: scaling data instead of engineering specialized solutions Agentic harnesses and robots executing multi-step, hour-long physical workflows GPT-6, coding agents, and AI-generated simulation environments for robotics research World-action models vs. VLAs, and why vision alone may not be enough Jason’s journey through AlphaGo, Penn, NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and the Eureka project Dyna’s research culture, deployment-first philosophy, and vision for millions of robots Jason Ma LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jason-ma-742224a2/ X: https://x.com/JasonMa2020 Dyna Robotics Website: https://www.dyna.co/ X: https://x.com/DynaRobotics Timestamps 00:00:00 Introduction and Dyna-2’s World-Action Model 00:03:08 Diffusion Transformers, Flow Matching, and Generalist Robots 00:08:19 The Robotics Data Bottleneck 00:13:50 Synthetic Data and Self-Improving World Models 00:16:51 Real-Time Inference and Model Distillation 00:19:45 Full-Stack Robotics: Hardware and Supply Chains 00:25:02 Why Dyna Built a Wheeled Semi-Humanoid 00:29:35 Teaching Robots New Tasks and Evaluating Performance 00:31:59 Autonomous Workflows and Hardware Limitations 00:36:06 Real-World Deployments at Best Western and Din Tai Fung 00:41:07 The Bitter Lesson of Robotics 00:46:13 Agentic Harnesses for Physical AI 00:49:07 GPT-6, Coding Agents, and AI-Native Robotics 00:52:02 World-Action Models vs. VLAs 00:59:17 From AlphaGo to Founding Dyna Robotics 01:04:20 Dyna’s Research Culture and the Future of Robotics Transcript Introduction: Jason Ma and Dyna Robotics Swyx [00:00:00]: All right, we’re here on site with Jason Ma, the co-founder, chief scientist of Dyna Robotics. Thanks for having us in your office. Jason Ma [00:00:06]: Of course. Thank you for coming. Vibhu [00:00:07]: It’s been a blast. We got to see—you’ll see plenty of B-roll—drinks being pulled, a lot of evals, robots with knives for the first time. So under the hood of all this you have a world action model. What is that? Dyna-2: A World Action Model That Predicts the Future Jason Ma [00:00:22]: So last month, we released our world action model called Dyna-2. So it’s the first world action model trained on more than one million hours of data. So going back to your question first, world action model is a model that’s able to predict the future video, the future state of the world, so hence the name world model. But in addition, you can also use that future generation to also produce actions robots can execute in the physical world to control the robot. So why do we do that? It’s a very powerful architecture, because if you think about how humans act in the physical world, in our brain, we are implicitly thinking about how the world will evolve based on our actions. So now we have a model architecture that’s able to do that to guide robot actions. So what we find is that by doing so, the model is much more dexterous, much more robust, and much more capable of generalizing to environments, to scenarios it’s never seen before. World Action Models: Inputs, Outputs, and Visual Reasoning Vibhu [00:01:17]: I wanna prompt this question a bit. I think a lot of people hear world model, and they think you’re outputting video or world or 3D state. You’re also doing action. I think most people don’t understand what models are under the hood of robotics. So what are the inputs and outputs? What’s the training data? What is the architecture? Give us all the details. Jason Ma [00:01:39]: So, for inputs, the most important input is video, right? You can think about videos that the robot is capturing with its cameras, right? So video or images of the past many seconds, that’s the input. But for robots, what’s really interesting is that robot also has a lot of actuators and joint encoders on itself. So the robot also knows, the angles of its joints. So those can also be inputs to this world model. That’s something that’s very different from just a pure video model that’s only looking at videos, right? So that’s the input. And additionally, for robots, you want to be able to talk to it, to instruct it to do different tasks, right? So you can also feed it language instruction. So those are what I consider the basic set of inputs that go into any robotics models, including world action models. And once we have that the output, at the basic level, it needs to output actions the robots can execute on the hardware. But in the case of world action model, what’s really interesting is that in addition to the actions, it can also output future video, right? So basically, you can almost output the future video or some representation of it first, and then use that to guide robot actions. So the way I think about it is this is kind of analogous to chain of thought, you know. And basically, the models are reasoning in the visual, the physics space, and then outputting actions. So that’s the key difference between world action models outputs versus other kind of models, robot models outputs. Diffusion Transformers, Flow Matching, and Smooth Actions Vibhu [00:03:08]: You put out a good blog post around your model. I think a lot of people understand language models or transformers, next-token predictors. In this case, you shared quite a bit. There’s diffusion, flow matching, you’re predicting next world state plus action. One thing you say is a million hours. How do you determine the architecture? Like, what are the choices there? What is the architecture? I feel like in language models, there’s a lot of take something off the shelf- Take trillions of tokens, do prediction, SFT, RL, and you have a model. What about this? How do you go from nothing to your model? Is there vanilla architecture off the shelf? Do you determine all this and what’s, what is the current state? Jason Ma [00:03:49]: Yeah, I think, yeah. So the mental framework to think about how do we build models for robotics is that there are essentially a couple things to look at. One is data, and the second is how do we make a model learn as much as possible from that data? So let’s first talk about the model actually, right? So the blog post we released is our Dyna-2 world action model. So under the hood is a diffusion transformer. The model uses an encoder-only transformer architecture. Vibhu [00:04:20]: Right, yeah. Jason Ma [00:04:20]: But what’s really interesting is that in visual domains, right, if you think about generating images, generating videos, and in this case, robots looking at images to generate actions, people have found the diffusion kind of architecture to work really well. So what is a diffusion model? A diffusion model is a model that takes some random noise and through iterative computation can go from noise to something that’s really high-dimensional, that’s something really highly defined and have very fine-grained feature. If you think about generating images, right, you want sharp edges, sharp corners, color contrast. And for robotics, even though you’re not generating image, you’re generating actions that needs to be very precise, very smooth, right? So it has kind of the same kind of consideration and desiderata as generating image. So that’s why from first principles, the whole field, not just us, have been using this kind of diffusion transformer architecture to train robotics foundation models. You need the transformer aspect because transformer is the thing that can just ingest the most amount of data, can learn. Then diffusion helps you to refine the outcome to get to the smooth, precise, fine-grained motion you need to actually execute on the robot. So that’s the architecture that goes behind a lot of our recent breakthroughs. Swyx [00:05:37]: And we’ve covered flow matching before on the podcast. It is mostly an efficiency speed-up. Like, let’s say you normally would take forty to a hundred diffusion steps. You can reduce it to four. Jason Ma [00:05:48]: Yeah, that’s right. So with the diffusion model, one thing that’s very hard in practice is that you need to tune the scheduler, like by how much you’re tuning or converting the initial noise input into the final output. So flow matching is kind of like a special case of diffusion that makes the transformation much simpler. In practice, you don’t have to tune as much, and it works just as well. That is why I think about two to three years ago, most generative modeling for image and video has shifted from a diffusion model to a flow matching model. But the concept is the same, and flow matching is just a special, simpler to tune, variant of diffusion. Yeah. Swyx [00:06:26]: It actually makes me think that. So flow matching obviously has trade-offs in quality. But actually, it’s very suited for action diffusion and robotics because you get to reevaluate in real time. Whereas in images, you are— it’s basically one shot. Jason Ma [00:06:40]: That’s right. Pretraining a Generalist Robot and Adapting to New Tasks Vibhu [00:06:41]: Which is pretty fun. We got to mess with the laundry folding robot … throw a random towel in. The models adapt, right? I think one key thing about your models is that they’re tr— they’re made to be generalists, so one foundation model and you adapt them a lot. How does that work? Basically, in 45 minutes of mapped data, you can generalize towards. We saw an example of pulling drinks out of a fridge. What’s the what’s the mindset there of one general model, and then how do you adapt to different tasks? Jason Ma [00:07:14]: So the way we think about it is that for robotics, we need to build a very general, strong base model, right? And then— Because if you think about how a human interacts and behaves in the physical world, right, we have very strong base knowledge. We can just readily do a lot of tasks. But if you want to become an expert at any given task, there is some amount of training that needs to happen. And I think to train a general-purpose robot like the one we’re building here, the same principle has to apply. So our approach is to first train a general model that’s training on as much data as we can find. So that is why in our Dyna-2 report, our model is trained over a million hours of human data as a starting point. And then given that strong foundation, what we found is we can quickly make the robot or make the model do many different tasks with a very minimal amount of fine-tuning to just tell the model, “Here’s the task I want it to do, and here’s very few amount of demonstrations,” and the model can readily do bunch of the tasks that you have seen in office. Yeah. A Million Hours of Data: Egocentric Video and Robot Demonstrations Swyx [00:08:19]: We actually have quite a few people who deal in data, who sell data. What is good data? What is bad data? What do you want to buy? I think that these are all open questions. Like, obviously, I think the top, important thing is egocentric data of humans doing tasks. What else would you modify on that basic statement? Jason Ma [00:08:42]: So I think data is the most important thing in robotics today, because unlike language model, there is no internet, right? So every company that’s building model, building hardware has to think about data. So there’s, roughly couple of different ways of operating here. One is that you can collect a lot of data yourself, which is what we are doing as well. Swyx [00:09:02]: You have employees here doing that. Jason Ma [00:09:04]: There are robots everywhere in the office, right? But if you think about how much data you need for robotic foundation model, I think the amount of data any individual company can collect by themselves is just nowhere near sufficient, right? It’s kind of like, you’re trying to build an internet by just having Reddit or just having Facebook. They’re great websites, a lot of users, but it’s not enough, right? So when we think about data, there has to be some sort of data acquisition happening, right? You buy data, you look at data that’s already out there. And then there’s many different tiers, right? You mentioned data quality. I think data quality in robotics is a non-stationary problem in the sense that what is high-quality data for your model changes over time. Like, when your model doesn’t know anything, like when it’s zero, any data is useful, right? You can use a lot of video data. In the case of egocentric data, I think it’s actually a very good way of pre-training robots because human data is so diverse. Like, it covers every single physical activity you can possibly imagine. And that gives robot, the model such a strong prior on how things, how the world can evolve around a embodied actor, human. But the issue with human data is that until your robot looks exactly like a human, there’s gonna be some gap between human actions and the robot actions, right? So just by training on human data, today, it’s not very likely you can just execute robot actions directly. So you still need some amount of adaptation using the robot’s own data, right? But the robot’s own data collected on a robot is gonna be much more expensive and much harder to collect. So the kind of recipe we’re thinking about is like, how do we take the largest source of data we have today, like egocentric data, to give the model a strong prior over everything physical manipulation can cover, and then combine that with a small amount of robotics data to make the robot master whatever task we’re interested in. So data quality and getting data in robotics is really, I think it’s a fascinating, multifaceted problem. But the reality is that there’s not a single winning strategy like, “Oh, here’s one kind of data. I’m only gonna collect on that,” Jason Ma [00:11:25]: Which will give you a strong foundation model. You really need to think about, “This human data covers this part of robot cognition I need. Robot data covers low-level reflex dexterity the robot also needs,” and put them into one model. And I think that’s what gives a really adaptable, really strong model at the end. Yeah. Data Partnerships and Specialized Training Examples Swyx [00:11:44]: I’ll prompt you, just for again, for the people listening who want to work with you. What, d— what data vendors do you want. This is your call for data. What- Jason Ma [00:11:55]: Yeah, no, that’s a great question. And yeah, so in our Dyna-2 blog, at the end, we actually have an email address called datapartnerships@dyna.co. So if you’re a data vendor that has a lot of high-quality, let it be egocentric data, robot data, video data, or anything you think could help robots, send it to that email. Our team will take a look, and we’ll get back to you. Swyx [00:12:16]: But at your stage, are you. You’re probably not buying any more egocentric data off the shelf, right? That you probably want to be like, “Here’s what I need. You go-” Vibhu [00:12:26]: Is there a niche that’s lacking? Swyx [00:12:28]: You need a Scale AI, you need a Mercor for doing this. I see. The custom data- Vibhu [00:12:32]: The folks that don’t work in robotics are probably thinking like, “Okay, some niche factory.” Like … you showed putting tubes in. There’s only so much data you’ll find about that but like would a lot of that help you? Jason Ma [00:12:43]: Yeah, no. If you really want to nail a task, having data from that task will certainly help you a lot, right? So for us, it’s like we still think, just a million hours of data is not enough. It’s just the beginning. Like, we showed the first model on a million-hour scale, but we need more than that right? So we are still looking at a lot of just raw, diverse data, that we can get. But we’re also thinking about how do we get more custom data either collected in-house or by our partner for really, specific niche tasks? items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.content: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied: Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git, migrations, version-control, ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, agentic-engineering

items.title: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine
items.author: niztk
items.content: Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs. I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data. Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction. How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur... The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b). Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next. The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored. Feedback welcome, especially on wrong answers and on questions it should handle but does not.

items.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
items.author: BrianKrebs
items.content: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027). At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system. While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug. Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs. “We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said. Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software. Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first. “Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said. Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.
