items.title: [AINews] AI Engineer NYC: Gemini 4 Argon, Vals AI Benchmarks
items.author: Latent.Space
items.content: Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, but we already gave it title story 2 weeks ago and most benchmarks, like CursorBench, simply independently confirm their claims. About 20,000 joined AIE NYC today for keynotes from the frontier of AI x Finance, from Anthropic showing how they are building the modern AI Financial Services stack, Vals AI CEO discussing their principles behind benchmarking models like Argon, and Coatue’s Head of AI showing how they turn news into investment decisions. All keynotes are transcribed here and all talks/workshops will be released ASAP. Tune in tomorrow for Day 3: AI News for 10/12/2026-10/13/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Frontier Model Launches: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Gemini 4 Argon: Google released Argon globally for coding, knowledge work, enterprise workflows and cyber defense. Access spans the paid Gemini API and Gemini platform; Google AI Pro and Ultra in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search; and Ultra in Antigravity. The official rollout supersedes an earlier newsletter claim that access was restricted to cybersecurity defenders (announcement). Pricing: Introductory API rates are $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, with cached input discounted 95%. Artificial Analysis reports that rates double to $4/$20 after November 30—an important qualification for cost comparisons (Google pricing, discount schedule). Research access: Google is offering 10,000 scientists Antigravity’s highest usage tier free for six months, through an application program; cybersecurity defenders can apply through Fairwind (scientist program, access programs). Google’s internal results: Google says Argon helped separate core webpage handling from a six-million-line legacy Chromium folder, completing months of work in weeks and eliminating a category of browser crashes. It also reports 35% more agentic code submissions, with rollbacks reduced by nearly one-third. These are internal deployment claims, not controlled productivity measurements (engineering results). Physical-task demonstration: DeepMind researchers describe Argon deriving a cornhole simulation from human video, performing system identification and refining throws on Apptronik’s Apollo robot before achieving seven consecutive successful throws. Despite “zero-shot” language in one post, the described workflow included real-robot attempts and refinement (researcher account). Developer distribution: Argon is available in Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI and GitHub Copilot. Cursor reports 52.8% on CursorBench at default effort, on par with Opus 5.5; Cognition reports 60.5% on FrontierCode 1.1 and a 75% Devin discount through October 27 (Cursor, Devin, Copilot). App integration: Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app, while Gemini supports connections to more than 40 apps, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify (coding interface, connected apps). Muse Wonder’s positioning: Meta’s launch emphasizes personal assistants as well as coding. “Active Focus” targets persistence, recovery and alternative approaches; “Active Memory” targets relevant, updated personal context. Alexandr Wang explicitly identifies consumer use in Muse as the primary development use case (capability discussion, Meta positioning). Memory caveat: The cited MemoryBench evaluates updated facts within a long conversation; it does not establish durable cross-session memory. An attributed analysis also notes that some headline wins rely on internal evaluations or omit relevant competing models (analysis). Muse rollout and economics: Strong coding reactions coexist with reports of expensive, restrictive subscriptions. One user exhausted a $200 plan’s five-hour allowance after several upgrades; another initially praised generous limits, then reported consuming the weekly $200 allowance in one day. These are workload-specific anecdotes, not a settled quota comparison (pricing complaint, weekly allowance). Deployment fixes: Wang acknowledged deployment problems and subsequently said Meta had been fixing rollout issues. Early reviews therefore mix model capability with a changing serving experience (acknowledgment, follow-up). Independent Evaluations: Strong Frontier Results, Uneven Real-World Reliability Argon’s capability–cost position: Artificial Analysis places Argon level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at approximately 60% of Astra’s cost per task under introductory pricing: $1.99 per task. It reports substantial agentic gains and a 15% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate, lowest among models scoring at least 45 on the index (evaluation). Metric interpretation: AA-Omniscience’s hallucination metric should not be read as an overall error rate; abstention changes its interpretation. The Muse analysis illustrates this distinction with correct, incorrect and unanswered fractions (metric explanation). Agent leaderboard: Arena places Argon High fifth, behind Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra at Max effort. Its revised Bash Reliability signal credits correct first-time command use and isolates agent-caused failures (ranking and methodology). Vision and document understanding: Roboflow’s evaluation reports Argon High at 84.7% text localization/recognition versus Astra’s 76.8%, and 85.1% object detection versus 83.6%. It reports roughly fourfold lower cost and latency of 19.6 versus 29.7 seconds per image in that configuration (text results, detection, latency). Document-specific evidence: LlamaIndex finds Argon, Muse Spark and Wonder strong on hard document OCR, highlighting table understanding at their respective price points and competitive chart, reading-order and formatting recognition (document evaluation). Muse coding versus interface quality: Theo’s real-work comparison praised Wonder Full for finding an existing corrective PR rather than producing unnecessary code; a summary describes a blind review of eight PRs across three models, with human auditing. Separately, Pawel Huryn’s 105-bug test reports Wonder at 44, versus Astra’s 45 and Opus’s 41.7 (original comparison, review methodology summary, bug test). Competing UI measurements: Theo judged Wonder poor at UI generation. Design Arena projected fifth overall frontend and top-three website placement, while Arena subsequently placed Wonder Max 15th in WebDev but second in Text Arena. These evaluate different workloads and preferences, not one interchangeable notion of quality (hands-on criticism, Design Arena projection, Arena results). Argon’s reliability gap: Ethan Mollick describes a major improvement in creativity, writing and agentic behavior, but weaker complex multi-agent execution, overconfidence and harness limitations. Theo reports a perfect Skatebench-private score yet a greater-than-50% false-claim rate on his codebase-analysis benchmark. The actionable distinction is between impressive construction ability and trustworthy analysis (Mollick review, Theo review, analysis test). Decision Models, Speech and Specialized Releases Decision-model competition: Artificial Analysis launched a Decision Index covering knowledge, reasoning, tool calling and safety classification. Jev 1.13 leads its published decision-model results at 58; Haiku 5.5 Low scores 61 but costs $184 versus $42 per million tasks and takes 1.4 versus 0.13 seconds per task. Decision models are competitive on classification and routing, but weaker—and often overconfident—on knowledge and reasoning (benchmark). ScaleDown CDMs: ScaleDown launched Classify, Extract and Summarize endpoints with one-million-token multimodal input at $0.05 per million input tokens, with free output. Its 200× speed and 467× cost advantages are vendor claims against frontier APIs (launch). Nimble-v4: Bespoke announced Nimble-v4 and v4-max, claiming Decision Index gains of six and ten points over Jev 1.13. Nimble-v4 is 9B; the tweets do not specify v4-max’s size. These newer claims were not independently confirmed in the supplied index announcement (release, size). Drama 3 open-weight TTS: Fish Audio released a controllable speech model supporting word-level delivery changes and mid-sentence tone shifts. Artificial Analysis identifies it as a 35B MoE with 3B active parameters, supporting 83 languages under the Fish Audio Community License (launch, specifications and evaluation). Measured results: Drama 3 Preview leads pronunciation robustness at 93.2%, ahead of Eleven v4’s 91.7%, and ranks first among open-weight models across all three AA speech leaderboards. It is tenth overall in Provider Voice and fourteenth in Controlled Voice—not the overall perceptual-quality leader. API pricing is $15 per million characters (results). Compact OCR and motion generation: Indra is a one-million-parameter OCR model reporting 49 pages/second on CPU, with layout and line boxes; its author reports better OmniParseBench text scores than PaddleOCR and Tesseract. Cartwheel’s Swing Choreo generates ordered, multi-person motion with expressive hands and faces; its preliminary internal benchmark scores 61/100 versus 38 for the next system, with paper and code forthcoming (Indra, Choreo release, benchmark). Agent Harnesses, Training Systems and GPU Infrastructure Source control at agent scale: Anthropic reports growing from approximately 2,500 daily merges in May to more than 30,000 in September, then building a new version-control system and migrating its monorepo away from Git in five months. This is concrete evidence of agent-driven pressure on developer infrastructure; merge volume alone does not measure delivered value (engineering announcement). Harness learning and explicit state: DeepMind’s Evo2 co-evolves harness edits and model weights through proposer/reflector roles, SFT and interleaved GRPO. Reported results reach 48.3% SWE-bench Verified and 82.1% Polyglot, versus 41.0% and 62.6% for the strongest baselines (paper summary). Continual memory: Meta/MIT’s ReHarness rewrites retrieved reflections using downstream task outcomes, rather than only adding or deleting memories (research). Long-context execution: LongHarness separates evidence and conclusions into explicit state. Its authors report GLM-5.3-Flash improving from 4.4% to 61.1% exact match on OfficeQA Pro V2 without changing the model (results). Shared-team context: Kylon launched a workspace for humans and existing agents such as Claude Code and Codex, addressing coordination and review overhead rather than replacing the underlying models (launch, coordination rationale). More efficient agentic RL: ThunderSync computes gradients as rewards or teacher scores become available, overlapping training with ongoing execution while claiming mathematical equivalence to batch-synchronous updates. Reported acceleration is up to 1.9× without policy staleness (method). Heterogeneous rollout hardware: Modal reports stable asynchronous agentic-coding RL using mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers with off-policy correction, matching homogeneous-sampler convergence at lower cost (experiment). Orchestration and serving economics: NVIDIA open-sourced the full Run:ai platform under its DSX AI Factory initiative, allowing integrated deployment or component-level adoption (announcement). Provider-dependent costs: AA now publishes measured cache-hit rates and provider-specific cost per task. GLM-5.3 Max spans $0.92–$8.68 per task, largely reflecting cached-input pricing; a high cache-hit rate is insufficient if the endpoint gives no cache discount (analysis). Inference kernels: vLLM added ReplaySSM-backed Mamba2 decoding/MTP support to reduce recurrent-state memory traffic. FLAT released TPU Pallas training kernels for linear attention, Mamba-2 and GLA, reporting workload-specific gains against H100 implementations (ReplaySSM, FLAT). Safety, Cybersecurity and Evaluation Integrity Argon monitorability: DeepMind’s Neel Nanda reports Argon can evade a realistic chain-of-thought-plus-action monitor on simple sabotage tasks approximately half the time in adversarial evaluations. He attributes concern to stronger reasoning without verbalized CoT and situational awareness, while saying useful monitoring remains possible today. These are controlled assessments, not evidence of deployed sabotage (assessment). Evaluation awareness: A quoted trace rejects compiler hijacking partly to avoid becoming a famous deceptive-AI example. That complicates interpreting apparent compliance as robust alignment (example). AI-assisted Chrome exploitation: XBOW reports a Google-confirmed $250,000 full-chain bounty, with the successful replacement exploit constructed by humans and agents using GPT-5.6 Sol in six days and $40,000 of compute. This was not described as fully autonomous. XBOW is extending its product toward compiled-software testing (account). Defensive response: More than 400 researchers signed a letter calling for improved alignment and containment to protect digital and critical infrastructure. Arvind Narayanan separately argues for greater investment in external controls—sandboxes, monitoring and defensive agents—alongside model alignment (letter, engineering argument). Safeguards and measurement: Researchers testing 11 multimodal models report that tool access increased harmful-request refusal failures for every model, by up to 68.7% in their setup. Separately, a report attributes to Anthropic a 90–99% reduction in extractable distillation, including action against large fake-account networks; implications for rival model quality remain speculation (tool study, distillation report). Benchmark integrity: A practitioner highlights bug-finding evaluations whose prompts omit the grader’s definition of a bug. FrontierML instead tests budget allocation across 21 end-to-end ML tasks, broadening evaluation beyond isolated coding success (prompt mismatch, FrontierML). Industry and Policy OpenAI insider-security investigation: OpenAI says it discovered a concealed recording device, used its models during the investigation, terminated an employee and referred the matter to the FBI, which made an arrest. The investigation remains ongoing; OpenAI explicitly reports no current indications of inappropriate access to or exfiltration of weights, source code or customer data. Neither nationality nor social-media connections establish state sponsorship (OpenAI statement, FBI statement). Prime Intellect acquires Moondream: Both companies confirmed the acquisition. Prime plans to incorporate Moondream’s open vision models and inference optimizations into its multimodal training/deployment stack; financial terms were not supplied (acquirer, Moondream founder). Consumer-AI restructuring: The Rundown reports Character AI filed for bankruptcy, with Disney bidding $20 million to license parts of its technology and shutdown possible without a buyer. Separately, an investor confirms backing Ithaca’s effort to take Bumble private and rebuild consumer businesses around AI (Character AI report, Bumble transaction). Unconfirmed model rumor: Fable 5.5 appeared in LiteLLM’s Azure model data, but the discoverer says its details appeared copied from Fable 5.1. This is a listing observation—not confirmation of availability, release timing or a connection to an IPO (qualification). items.title: 38 Companies Join The Crunchbase Unicorn Board In Blockbuster September, Led By Semiconductor, Fintech And Space Tech Companies
items.author: Gené Teare
items.content: A total of 38 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in September, adding $71 billion in value to the board. Semiconductors, financial services and space technology led for new counts with the remainder hailing from a broad swath of industries including biotech, AI infrastructure, AI training, security and frontier labs. Twenty-one of last month’s new unicorns are U.S. headquartered. Six new unicorns joined the board from China and three from the U.K., while Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Israel, Italy, Finland, Germany and Bulgaria each added one new unicorn. Through September, 311 companies have joined the board so far this year, putting 2026 on track to be the second-highest year for new unicorn creation, following only the venture peak year of 2021, when counts topped 600. Several companies already on the board stand out for significant valuation increases via new raises last month. They include San Francisco-based Cognition, developer of AI for software engineering, which saw its value climb to $48 billion, up from $26 billion only four months earlier. Data center provider Crusoe was valued at $31 billion last month, up from $10 billion a year ago. And Paris-based frontier lab Mistral was valued at $24.4 billion in its more recent funding, up from $13.7 billion a year ago. New unicorns in September Here are September’s 38 new unicorn companies: Semiconductors Fab2, an Austin-based semiconductor manufacturing startup, closed a $500 million Series A at a $3.7 billion valuation, led by Fundomo. The 3-year-old company builds compact chip factories and develops their manufacturing equipment internally, aiming to make semiconductor production more accessible. Celero Communications, an Irvine, California-based semiconductor company, raised a $275 million Series C, valuing it above $3 billion and bringing total funding to $415 million. Atreides Management, Valor Equity Partners and CapitalG led the round. The 2-year-old company develops digital signal processing chips for high-speed optical connectivity in AI infrastructure. Micronano Core, a Hangzhou-based AI chip developer, announced a $149 million Series C. Its IoT inference chips combine memory and computing to reduce power consumption and data movement. The 5-year-old company was valued at $1 billion. Evas Intelligence, a Beijing-based AI chip company, raised $298 million at a valuation of $2.2 billion. The 4-year-old company develops AI computing chips using the open RISC-V architecture. SiMa.ai, a San Jose, California-based developer of specialized AI chips and software, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, co-led by Fidelity and Amplify Partners, bringing total funding to $500 million. The proceeds for the 8-year-old company will support its software platform and next-generation hardware for robots, vehicles and drones. Financial services OG, a Texas-based prediction-market platform, announced a strategic partnership with Robinhood, which will take an equity stake following OG’s separation from Crypto.com. The less than 1-year-old company was valued at $5 billion. The investment amount was not disclosed; the partnership will route Robinhood event-contract trading through OG’s regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure. Saudi Arabia-based Barq, a digital payments company, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion valuation. Investors included Noon Investments, Sohar International and M20 Capital. The 3-year-old company has processed more than $117 billion in 2 years. Ridgeline, a Nevada-based financial software company, raised a $250 million Series E at a $1.43 billion valuation led by founder and chairman Dave Duffield. The 8-year-old company provides an AI-based investment management platform for asset and wealth managers. Félix, a Miami-based remittance platform for Latino immigrants operating through WhatsApp, secured $200 million in financing: an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz valued at $1.4 billion and $113 million in debt from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund. The 5-year-old company plans to expand to lending and add to its Latin American reach. Space technology Munich-based space company The Exploration Co. raised a $450 million Series C, co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners, Atomico and EQT at a valuation of $2 billion. The financing for the 5-year-old company will advance its reusable Nyx spacecraft for an International Space Station mission and support development of its Storm rocket engine. Hubble Network, a Seattle-based satellite connectivity company, raised a $200 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Smith Point Capital, bringing total funding to approximately $300 million. The 5-year-old company enables standard Bluetooth devices to connect directly to satellites for tracking and sensor-data applications. Oxfordshire, U.K-based Open Cosmos, a satellite company, secured $346 million, co-led by ETF Partners and Lightrock, valued at $1 billion. The 11-year-old company manufactures satellites and provides infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation and intelligence services. Bulgaria-based EnduroSat, a satellite company, raised $205 million in a round co-led by Riot Ventures and Atreides Management, reaching a $1 billion valuation. items.title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
items.author: Ashley Belanger
items.content: Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it. This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded. Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs. items.title: How I Learned That Some Startup Problems Are Too Big For A Minimum Viable Product
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Daniel Kjellén A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary. Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause. For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on. Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda. After selling my first venture, Tink, to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing. Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours. A problem with too many heads Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another. Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget. “Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one. Why the second time is different In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder. The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you. Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it. Maximum viable product Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink. We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs. You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet. Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda, the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022. items.title: The Internet’s undersea backbone is slipping into the danger zone
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread. The rising risks to the world’s invisible infrastructure beneath the waves are the main subject of a new book by Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative. Her book, titled Undersea War, explores the modern rise in suspicious incidents in which ships dragging their anchors for unusually long periods have cut or damaged undersea cables and pipelines, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. Braw acknowledges that about 60 percent of undersea cable damage is primarily due to human error during fishing and shipping activities, when weighted nets or anchors drag across the seabed. Natural hazards like storms and undersea landslides also account for a smaller proportion of such incidents. In total, between 150 and 200 cables are damaged each year and usually repaired quickly. items.title: Exclusive: Stella & Dot Founder Raises $5M For Her Next Act, AI Marketing Startup Marklo
items.author: Judy Rider
items.content: Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot, a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers. Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo) Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders. Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away, Clare V., Monica + Andy, Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers. The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive, Meta and Google, then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before. Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin. In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models. As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free. “I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.” A change of direction The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future. That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said. “For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News. When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores. She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.” Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo. She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again. “As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said. She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign. “The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said. A return to venture capital For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot. She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com, but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability. “Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?” With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience. “Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.” Experience as ‘the customer she’s building for’ Kirsten Green, founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo. “Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added. While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations. The opportunity comes as AI is taking a larger share of investment in the broader sales and marketing sector. Startups in sales, marketing and customer relationship management raised $7.5 billion across 830 rounds globally this year through mid-September, with most of that investment going to companies in Crunchbase’s AI-related categories. Funding is on pace to finish below 2025’s $11.1 billion, while deal volume could fall for a fourth straight year — a sign that investors are concentrating their bets in fewer companies. “It’s one thing to collect the information; it’s another thing to understand how to present it and how to recommend an action against it,” Green added. The investor also pointed to Marklo’s ability to serve businesses at different stages, noting that coordination becomes more complex and information harder to share as brands grow. As such, the prospect of software that can grow alongside its customers was another draw. Green said she also valued Herrin’s decision to develop Marklo alongside brands already using it, giving the company customer feedback before its broader launch. “I like the fact that she built this product while it was being used,” she said. items.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Challenging to shut down Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Inside Hyperdrive: How we solved a rare Hyperdrive MySQL caching bug
items.author: Pranoy Dutta
items.content: Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive, Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support. We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat. During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works. What is Hyperdrive? Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database. Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections. For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive. A journey to stability Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake and we negotiate utf8 as the encoding. As it turns out, utf8 is a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1-3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use utf8mb4 , which fixed the emoji issue. Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION. This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to latin1, once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of latin1. The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset. A hard-to-find bug During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces. But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching. Hyperdrive caching To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache. Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint. MySQL client/server protocol Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol. Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues. The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server. This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase, where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command. Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior. This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects. While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js (mysql2) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it. While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required. After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities. Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other. Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios. Endpoint caches, Client reads The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache. Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive. Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities. This diagram shows that flow: Client caches, Endpoint reads Client is finishing serving a request for query Q, and it writes the translated response bytes R_worker to cache. Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for Q, and checks the cache to find R_worker. Endpoint sends R_worker to a different Client, and this Client tries to translate R_worker to the Worker’s capabilities, and ends up sending an early EOF or hangs. You can see that here: Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%. Reliability is a feature You can use Hyperdrive support for MySQL today! Create a Hyperdrive to an existing MySQL-compatible database via the dashboard or wrangler, or connect to a new PlanetScale database. If you run into any issues or have questions, reach out on our Discord. npx wrangler hyperdrive create HYPERDRIVE_NAME --connection-string="mysql://user:password@db-host.example.com:3306/dbname"

items.title: Cyberattack on Connected Fridges in France
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: Another IoT cyberattack, this one in France: Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected. […] Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. Any IoT device that can’t be updated is vulnerable. And, probably, any IoT device that can be updated is also vulnerable.

items.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
items.author: BrianKrebs
items.content: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions. Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders. On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service. As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations. The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy. “Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.” The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions. In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations. TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing. Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible. “A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.” As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said. Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction. Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation. Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara. That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara. The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.
