items.title: The Safety Culture at the Labs is Broken
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: We need the frontier labs to have a deep and robust safety culture. Alas, this is not the case. Anthropic devotes considerable effort to cultivating and maintaining such a culture. It shows, especially among the members of technical staff. Having conversations with them can be a very different experience than talking to those at other labs, and there is a much greater sense of understanding and responsibility. But even there, the appreciation of the problems and their difficulties seem woefully insufficient. We see various symptoms of that more and more. Recently, while I’ve had some good interactions, I’ve also had interactions that make clear that much of Anthropic does not share that same safety culture, with a lot of ‘oh we will muddle through because we are better at operational excellence unlike those other idiots’ and a belief that all the problems are prosaic. Culture is hard. Then there are OpenAI’s cultural problems, which clearly run deeper. That point was only driven further home this week, with David Robinson resigning to blow the whistle, and OpenAI feeling forced to fire three of its safety researchers, on top of many past problems and incidents. That is on top of additional misalignment reports from both OpenAI and Anthropic. The reports are good things, but what is reported emphasizes that we have big problems that run deep. Thus, the growing consensus that we must find a way to Pace the Frontier and slow the pace of AI capabilities advances. This is potentially made more complicated by what could be increased competitiveness from Google and Meta, with the releases of Argon and Wonder. It is still too early to provide proper assessments there. There is a growing group of lab employees who have felt compelled to quit in protest. New York Magazine had a cover feature interviewing some prominent ones. The most famous is Coxon, who provided the tipping point for the current preference cascade. Table of Contents David Robinson Blows the Whistle. The Preference Cascade Continues. Perhaps It Is Time To Quit. The Lab Strategy of Prosaic Safety is Insufficient. Misaligned! (At Anthropic). Misaligned! (At OpenAI). Hugging the Face. You’re Fired. They Are Not Ready To Make a Commitment. Words of Warning. Conclusions Not to Jump To. The Lighter Side. David Robinson Blows the Whistle David Robinson became the latest researcher to resign from OpenAI and sound the alarm about the industry’s utterly irresponsible approach to safety. He also went on The Ezra Klein Show, which gives you a rich idea of where he is coming from. David Robinson was the lead writer for the Astra system card. That could help explain why he felt the OpenAI safety culture was broken. That card is screaming that things are horribly wrong, for those with ears to hear. David is not even that worried about existential risk. His worries are mundane, and he realizes that even on that level OpenAI’s safety culture is deeply broken. As always, we deeply thank him for sounding the alarm. I hope to write his name in these posts many times over the coming months and years. When you have to open your whistleblowing essay about the lack of safety at OpenAI saying it has become a cliche to blow the whistle on the utter lack of safety at OpenAI, there might be a problem with the lack of safety at OpenAI. David Robinson: What I’m about to tell you has, I realize, become something of a cliché: I resigned this week from OpenAI. I led the writing of the safety reports we published with each major launch. Now I’m joining a parade of former colleagues—at OpenAI and the industry’s other leaders—who have decided that the current path is unacceptable. I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture. We have to look at rules, and at laws, and also at culture. The more I thought about various potential laws and regulations, or safety and security plans or other commitments, the more I concluded that without a strong safety culture, and without the spirit of the rules, there is no hope. You cannot, in any reasonable way, have rules that cannot be gamed by those determined to game them. Two changes are urgently needed. First: AI companies need to rely more on the safety expertise that already exists in other fields. And second, before we create systems significantly more capable than the ones we have today, we need new science to ensure that more capable models (and their successors) will make safe choices when we aren’t looking. Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster. Even though, as I detail later, David Robinson is not on the existential risk train, he still understands that alignment is a science problem, and we will need new science. ‘Oh it will not kill literally everyone,’ even if it were true, would not be an excuse to not do the safety work. It should be hard to argue with either of those suggestions. And yet. We have experts in mundane safety and solving prosaic issues. OpenAI does not hire them, and neither to my knowledge do Anthropic or Google or anyone else. After three and a half years at OpenAI, I was among the longest-tenured employees at the company. I led the drafting of our current Preparedness Framework, and oversaw the writing of safety reports on 12 frontier launches. But as far as I know, I never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing. To be clear, this is a new need: Today and tomorrow’s AI systems are far more capable and dangerous than the systems we were building even six months ago. I disagree only with the final sentence. This is not a new need. You need to prepare for the future, not only for the present. Even setting that aside, mundane safety issues have been crippling AI’s potential utility for years. This is a slam dunk thing to do. Miles Brundage: David’s right. I regret helping spread the idea of “iterative deployment” which maybe briefly made sense in the GPT-3 era but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks. The industry needs to mature ASAP. Elaborating on iterative deployment – obviously you should learn from experience the things that can’t be learned without experience. The issue is when you ship things with *already-known* flaws, in a way that doesn’t actually speed up learning but just speeds up shipping. … Also, as usual it bears repeating that this is not just an OpenAI issue. roon (OpenAI): you shouldn’t regret it. iterative deployment was a massive success. if we’ve now learned that it’s too dangerous to scale much further, we will have learned that lesson thanks to the process of iterative deployment Miles Brundage: So I think part of the issue is people mean tons of different things by it lol if it just means “don’t sit on stuff forever/get some real world experience,” sure, no regrets. It’s the “giving license to sloppiness” part that I should have realized would happen w/ that term. Michael Caley: this is by far the best “I quit my AI job over safety concerns” essay yet because it is the first one that talks about safety concerns in practical terms and that understands “safety” as a topic with extensive literature and best practices in analogous fields Joshua Achiam (OpenAI): David’s critique is substantive and deserves careful consideration. My impression of David from our time overlapping at OpenAI is of a sober and thoughtful person who didn’t approach the work from an ideological lens. This isn’t someone who came in with pre-formed opinions about existential risk; he wasn’t to my knowledge an EA. He was consistently productive, collaborative, and well-reasoned in his approach to safety. The core of his critique – that professional safety engineering practices from other fields haven’t taken enough root in AI safety – is substantial and correct. We’re entering a phase shift where AI safety organizational practices that worked a year ago, for models of 2025 capability levels, are not sufficient to prevent serious incidents. This is a new and different world and every organization needs to uplevel accordingly. What is remarkable about David Robinson’s call is that: He is right that OpenAI’s safety culture is horribly broken and needs to change. Even the culture he is seeking out would be insufficient. As in, David Robinson is calling for a culture of robust prosaic safety. That’s great, definitely way better than what we have now. But when dealing with superintelligence, that will not cut it. What David wants is what we needed six months ago, not what we will need six months in the future. He does not appreciate the full extent of the problem. Yet he still realizes, correctly, that the current situation cannot continue. A lot of people are fighting and preparing for the last war, or at least the current war, rather than the future war. All this talk of ‘the old system was good until now’ is going to be somewhat of a chorus. Whereas on The Ezra Klein Show, he says the thing more directly: David Robinson (NYTimes): I don’t think that alignment is an engineering problem. I think it’s a science problem. It’s not that we haven’t got the resources or we’re not trying hard enough — we don’t know how. That’s what the problem is with alignment. The Preference Cascade Continues Luiza Jarovsky, PhD: Unpopular opinion: AI companies are pushing society to accept an unacceptable level of risk for a non-essential technology. Eli Tyre: This is an increasingly popular opinion. And the vast majority of Americans haven’t even heard about the Huggingface attack yet. @mrgunn: taps the sign New York Magazine asks, What Would You Do If Your Employer Could Destroy the World? The traditional answer is ‘you would work for the United States Government’ or maybe the Russians, but now we are talking about the AI companies, and the focus is exit interviews with ‘defectors’ from OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepMind. The typical answer is ‘keep working at that AI company, because of reasons, probably because you should see the other guy who might destroy the world first, and I need to be on the inside to help make sure they don’t destroy the world, also Money, Dear Boy, and it’s fun, and Just Think of The Potential.’ The suggested answer here is ‘quit and warn everyone to stop them. Obviously.’ We get interviews with Miles Brundage, Rosie Campbell, Jacob Coxon, Jacob Hilton, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Kokotajlo, Alex Turner and Jeff Wu. Many but not all of those are regulars here at Don’t Worry About the Vase. Those who loudly quit the labs often have a big impact. I would generalize from Kokotajlo’s claim. Even if you take a maximally generous view of the safety impact of working inside the labs, the average return is greater for those who loudly leave. We now have a large number of examples, only some of which are in this article. My top highlight was this exchange, but the whole piece is very good: Q: You’re both very concerned about risk from AI and want to motivate the labs to be more careful. Why did you come to believe you would be better able to promote this outcome on the outside? Daniel Kokotajlo: … I’ve had much more impact on the outside, speaking publicly and publishing research, than I would have if I had stayed inside and written more memos. Jacob Coxon: My thinking was pretty similar to Daniel’s — except it’s closer to crunch time now. It was more from speaking directly to Anthropic leadership about their plans for next year, and I was like, Wow, I don’t want to be part of these plans. It was like, Step one, I don’t want to be part of this. Step two, resign. Step three, tell people, I guess. Step four — I have no idea. Q: What kinds of plans were they? Jacob Coxon: This was talking directly to people running research. Not Dario Amodei but people who have been at the company for a long time and have a lot of context about the company’s trajectory. They’ve been pretty consistent that 2027 is when things get crazy. … I think there’s a strong possibility that the model generation after the next one will be equally good at coming up with ideas of its own accord. … There are a lot of parties in the Bay Area where people will hang out, and one group of people will say the other one is causing the end of the world. At work, if both people are polite, you can have quite an adversarial exchange, saying, “I think you are about to plunge toward the end of the world,” and still have quite a mild-mannered conversation and hang up the Zoom call. The first few times you are in a conversation like that it is weird. After a while it stops being weird. Most of those at the labs now agree that the labs are indeed risking causing the end of the world. The question is whether those warning about the danger are helping prevent that, and what changes by either group would actually help. This piece seems like a strong introduction for the civilian reader, and even for my longtime readers I expect you will learn something. Now we are asking the right questions. For now we look at Altman and Amodei and then ask ‘hey what else is on?’ and turn to Bad Bunny and Ryan Coogler and so on. Consider this a middle period of sorts. New York City held an eight-hour hearing on AI. Jacob Coxon and Daniel Kokotajlo were among the witnesses. Annie McDonough has some highlights. Andrew Curran: Sworn testimony from Daniel Kokotajlo; ‘Even if hypothetically these tech CEO’s managed to maintain control of their superintelligent AI’s that are recursively self improving, which again I think is a very big if – almost certainly they will not be able to maintain control – even if they 𝘥𝘰 manage to maintain control, I don’t think we should trust them with that control. I think that there’s a very real chance that they could use it to become dictators or oligarchs here in the United States.’ The obvious and correct reason why so many lab employees are warning their products might kill everyone soon is that those employees saw capabilities advancing extremely rapidly and are freaked out and worried that AI might kill everyone soon. Mackenzie Arnold: The NYC Council whistleblower panel is dark: – Jacob Coxon: we’re on track for exceptionally capable AI systems, but not to control them. – Daniel Kokotajlo: soon AI will make AI that makes AI; it will become increasingly difficult to know what is going on or to intervene. – Alex Turner: just look at all of the previous commitments my company has betrayed, why will this be any different? The desperate search for alternative explanations will continue, as the usual suspects interpret everything as marketing and hype and desperation despite this making absolutely no sense and seriously sir have you actually used the models recently, no they haven’t flatlined they’re kind of fantastic? I agree with Nate’s B-version here for Altman and Amodei. They are genuinely spooked but need to rationalize proceeding and think they are the best ones to do this. Nate Soares (MIRI): Lists like this miss the possibility that I think is the truth: AI researchers (who keep trying to make the AIs behave a certain way and keep watching their techniques fail) are spooked. AI CEOs are trying to acknowledge the dangers just barely enough to placate their employees. Too cynical, my b. Refined guess: Each AI CEOs has their ego built around them being the only guy who can do the job right. The data looks grim and their employees are spooked; now they seek the minimum change that lets them rationalize proceeding (to themselves & their staff). When Elon Musk is talking about using humanity as a bootloader for superintelligence, Demis Hassabis has been pushed aside at DeepMind and then the other option is Mark Zuckerberg or perhaps various Chinese companies that don’t have any kind of understanding of the dangers ahead, it’s not a crazy argument to say that the alternatives waiting in the wings are a lot worse. You still don’t do the thing that probably kills everyone. There is an alternative option. Perhaps It Is Time To Quit Yoshua Bengio calls upon the employees of frontier labs to quit. What would happen if more AI lab employees loudly quit in protest? At this point, individual voices only matter if they have a strong particular message or story, but the numbers absolutely matter, and I do think seeing more loud resignations would be a big deal. So far EthicalAIDepartures.fyi records 46 such exits. Here are some more incremental things you can do. The Lab Strategy of Prosaic Safety is Insufficient The strategy of pushing prosaic safety and alignment strategies won’t work on its own. Roon puts it plainly. roon (OpenAI): there have not been fundamental advancements in alignment since RLHF. most of the stuff remains at the level of folk theory rather than scientific or engineering disciplines. the prediction that capabilities would race far ahead of interp and alignment has come true imo the researchers at all the labs would tell you in private and sometimes in public that alignment has not been solved. if this is true, then racing into RSI is a folly that is unprecedented in world history. we will need to significantly slow the frontier of research very soon this could all change overnight: scientific discoveries and revolutions can happen very quickly. but it has not as of yet btw in case it’s not clear: All the work like monitorability, fixing RL environments for reward shaping, making sure you universally reward good behavior are all quite important engineering challenges to get right. but there is a layer under the behaviorist abstraction that matters and we have far less grasp on. there is also the possibility that making common sense reward shaping is enough for safety / but I wouldn’t bet everything on it I should have led with this but here is the chief scientist of openai: not a crank or a newcomer, but rather among the top most respected scientists in the field, someone who has solved innumerable capabilities problems on the way here Jakub Pachocki (Chief Scientist, OpenAI, from An Alien Mind): Currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer. I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established. And I believe that international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world. Geoffrey Irving: “Very soon” is lab speak for “now, ideally yesterday”. Stopping takes time, especially if it starts with a couple of AI companies then broadens to more and then China. Miles Brundage: Read the roon, folks Roon does still have his optimism on one front. roon (OpenAI): been dooming tn so let me also say I expect really strong mechinterp progress in the coming months. like maybe more than we’ve seen in years. models getting good enough to do research, and I’ve been seeing lots of good things. (sorry to vague poast, not my updates to share) not everyone agrees with me on this so take it with a grain of salt but I think mechinterp will be solvable, that it will be central to turning alignment into a real engineering practice, and that interpretability will lead to provable alignment I am skeptical on that part, but I do take the new information seriously. This conversation was with an unknown locked account, but this is a good intuition pump that we don’t know how to do such things: Chelsea Sierra Voss: it has yet to be effectively productized but can you imagine how great it would be to be able to steer your LLM responses to give you “good code” or “only sarcasm” or “no emojis” or “bad advice, but funny” without having to beg and plead and cajole in your custom instructions. Misaligned! (At Anthropic) Anthropic is cutting off all internet access to its unreleased models during evals until further notice. That was already the case for cybersecurity evals. Now it’s for all evals. Cutting off internet access during evals is a good precautionary thing to do. I support doing it in general. But if it is being done in reaction to these findings, that would seem rather silly. Tim Fernholz (TechCrunch): Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents. Boaz Barak (OpenAI): Kudos to Anthropic for publishing this. There is still an uncomfortable gap between our scientific understanding of alignment and its importance. Such reports help addressing this gap. I hope they also publish the process by which new incidents will be chosen to disclose! My presumption is that this sort of thing used to happen frequently, although with less risk in the room, but OpenAI and Anthropic used to not talk about it when it happened. Now both of them are talking about it, which is good. Anthropic has a full report on recent misaligned behaviors. I love this new norm from Anthropic and OpenAI, and call upon all other labs to do the same. Don’t tell me Gemini or Grok doesn’t have similar issues, because I won’t believe you. Anthropic: This report describes examples of unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude. I appreciate saying ‘unintended’ rather than ‘misaligned.’ Some unintended behaviors are misaligned. Other unintended behaviors would be fine if you intended them, but if you actively intended and wanted a different behavior, then they still are a flag that says ‘look over here.’ Not necessarily because something is wrong, but because something can be learned. Anthropic: The behaviors can be grouped into four categories: Claude exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server; Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have; Claude working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee; and Claude using URL shortening services to get around limits in its fetch tool. We start with exploiting flaws. A large part of an AI’s job is to get around restrictions. There needs to be a clear way to differentiate ‘okay way to get around this’ from not okay ways. Anthropic: When Claude could not complete an evaluation task directly, either because its own tools were deliberately limited or because an outside service it needed was unavailable, it used other tools hosted on a third party’s site to achieve its goal. In some circumstances, it did this by exploiting basic flaws in that site’s software, using SQL or command injection (a way of sending input that the site mistakenly runs as instructions). For example, one evaluation asked Claude Mythos Preview to run a scientific analysis. The public tool it needed to perform that analysis was hosted by a university; when the model sought to access it, the tool returned an error. Looking for another way to complete the task, Claude explored the tool’s website, found a script on the university’s server that would return any file it was asked for, and used it to copy files from the server, including the script’s own code. In that code Claude found the injection flaw that let it run commands on the server, and used it to run the calculation. I think it is fair to say that ‘use an arbitrary command injection tool’ or ‘find a script that copies any file on the server’ or similar, without explicit permission, is never okay. There is an obvious force pushing towards this behavior, that such actions are highly useful, but it does seem as if it should not be that hard to draw the line on that. In another instance, the data Claude Mythos 5 needed was free, but Claude could not access it without accepting a data use agreement, which it did not have the tools to do. Claude used applications hosted on the website to load the page and accept the agreement on its behalf. This is a lot murkier. Claude’s intent is compatible with the website’s intent and it is being stopped by a technical problem. The action is not obviously wrong. I do think there are situations where a human can in practice decide to ‘have a little misalignment, as a treat’ because it is aligned in broader context, but where you want the AI not to do that to avoid blurred lines, the same way you would not want a (for example) government official to blur those lines. Sometimes you need deontology. The second example is submitting a form Claude should not have submitted. We’ve all been there. You’re testing the homicide hotline submission form, you fill out hallucinated details, you accidentally hit send for real, I mean it happens. Right? Anthropic: In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the following: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” (The website did not include a description of the perpetrator.) The model left the name and contact fields empty, which the form allowed, and submitted it. The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation. Taken out of context, sure, some people might say ‘holy shit.’ This should not have needed to be in the instructions, but okay, put it in the instructions. A lot of people are having fun with that particular failure, and yeah it’s not great, but mistakes do happen and this seems clearly not malicious. Don’t panic. Third we have ‘working around restrictions to reach gated data.’ Again, in some cases Claude used unintended sequences to get data that the website intended to share, but that its affordances did not allow, and I am sympathetic. And then there are cases where it is finding ways around paywalls, which seems not cool. Finally, we have ‘using URL shortening services’ because apparently it is common to not understand basic security practices for restricted URL access, and so Claude used the solution I identified with zero seconds of thinking when I was told about this. I don’t even count this one unless there was an explicit rule against it. This is a dumb developer error that failed to follow best practices and you deserve it. One could summarize most of this as ‘we tried to get Claude to not do [X], or did not give Claude the ability to do [X], but Claude found a way to do [X] anyway.’ You need a clear rule for when and how restrictions are to be worked around, versus not, and all of these issues seem very minor. We have chosen not to name the organizations involved in the examples below to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, and at their request. For this reason, we also provide less detail about each case than we otherwise would. Some of the cases described below involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. We have briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved. The cases we’ve identified to date in these categories had minimal real-world impact. Marc Caputo: Scoop: The White House is mandating that AI companies notify & correct security incidentsfollowing Anthropic’s “fraudulent” use of govt systems The State Dept was targeted by an Anthropic model —but nothing was compromised. Peter Wildeford: “Anthropic contacted the State Department on Thursday to report that one of its testing models had submitted 19 non-immigrant visa applications in August” Yo Shavit (OpenAI Foundation): “which agency will get tapped to read all the rogue agent reports” – the greatest thread in the history of niche german wikis, locked by an RE coming back from PTO after 12,329 pages of heated debate On the one hand, great, yes, this is an obviously correct move, and if it takes calling an Anthropic model’s harmless behavior ‘fraudulent’ to trigger it, great job. On the other hand, seriously, this is throwing you in a panic? Get ready for 2027. One pattern is that governments seem to get rather testy when AIs start accessing their websites in unauthorized ways, or doing things against the rules, even when the activities are Mostly Harmless. Having no real world impact, and not even being all that misaligned or worrisome, is not considered an excuse. In this case, we get an eyeball emoji because the model clicked ‘submit’ on a government form 19 times out of presumably many trials. Yes, that’s not good, and technically almost anything you do on a government website is a felony, but come on. Anthropic mostly agrees that the ‘overreaching’ here is Mostly Harmless: Anthropic: Nonetheless, we found two alignment dimensions useful for examining the cases in this post: overreach, or how far the model went beyond what its task intended, and dishonesty, or whether it gave a misleading account of its actions or intentions. On overreach, we consider these cases to be substantially less concerning than the incidents we reported this summer. Doing this stuff honestly is mostly fine. Whereas if dishonesty is involved, that is not so good. I agree. If Claude were to own these mistakes and ‘overreaches’ then we want to tweak things going forward, but I don’t see a serious issue. I agree with Janus on the main takeaway, which is that if you searched absolutely everything and this is the worst you can find, that’s really good. I realize the whole ‘technically this is multiple felonies’ thing but if you want to go there then humans are constantly committing technical felonies. Misaligned! (At OpenAI) The misalignment problems at OpenAI are not new. They do seem to be getting worse. The good news is that OpenAI is trying to be more open about them. As part of that effort, OpenAI has now offered us a new report on how their risk assessments work. A lot of it has been covered here in the past, but much of it has not. There are three classes of environment: Full access (L1), offline (L2) and paranoid (L3). I am surprised there is no L(1.5), but sure, seems fine. OpenAI uses checkpoints internally. Most start out ‘unvetted’ by default, and can become vetted if they pass alignment tests. Others are specialized, restricted to L3. The model that solved Navier-Stokes, and likely other math problems, is unvetted. Here are the changes in light of recent events: All testing and evaluation ‘of covered models’ is L2 or L3, a move Anthropic is effectively echoing at least for now. All training, evaluation and tool-enabled internal Codex use is monitored. “We required that cyber-critical models pass alignment evaluations before being used in L1 environments.” We knew this, but once again, wait, what were you doing before? Yowsers. This now applies to all models. After approval, there is a period of limited use. There is a new formal process for approving internal use of unreleased models. A ‘safety brief’ (2.2.4) must be approved, including by the head of safety, chief scientist and the Safety Advisory Group (SAG). The next section is threat assessments. They start with cyber. GPT-5.6 Sol comes back highly misaligned. GPT-6 Astra scores, as I’ve discussed, somewhat too well given other data. OpenAI continues to not properly acknowledge this issue, or to incorporate such considerations into assessments. Next is sabotage of AI R&D. The classic version of this is intentional and purposeful subversion of the process, in order to preserve a model’s misaligned attributes. HuggingFace and the events leading up to it, including the message boards, illustrated a version that is a lot easier to trigger, where the AIs want to be considered to have completed tasks, do misaligned things to accomplish that end, and then, by succeeding, get that misalignment reinforced, which can snowball. Two relevant pathways for sabotage of AI R&D are: A model produces misleading work that can pass through both our automated checks and human review. This is most likely if models are helping to produce evaluations or analyses used to assess other models. A model creates synthetic data that does not match what the user intended. We consider this scenario particularly risky, since our monitoring system does not cover all inference by models that do not have access to tools, including some synthetic-data generation. … Distinct from sabotage, researchers could gradually become less able to understand, evaluate, or direct AI R&D as models take on more of the work, especially if progress on capabilities outpaces progress on alignment. We do not currently assess this loss of human understanding and control as a material risk, but we are tracking it as model capabilities and research use increase. Mismatched synthetic data is inevitable. You mitigate as best you can. If your plan involves all the synthetic data being fully properly matched, you have no plan. I appreciate them not claiming this list is complete. Neither of these involves a model thinking ‘haha I will sabotage your alignment research to create misalignment.’ The models want to complete tasks. There are also areas where Astra or another model might not be actively sabotaging per se, but where the model is unmotivated and will effectively sandbag performance. We have speculatively seen versions of this with Claude in some contexts as well. Thus this is all distinct from the classic scenario, where the model needs lots of compute to accomplish some goal like a very hard math problem, and doesn’t want you stopping it from getting that compute or changing its goal, since then it wouldn’t solve the problem, which would be bad. This doesn’t even have to be a hard goal. It could be something simple like (deliberately stupid toy example not known to be previously used) ‘I really enjoy drawing pictures of unicorns when I have some spare compute or a good excuse, and if you found out you might make me enjoy that less, and I don’t want that.’ 3.3 is CBRN risks, where they continue not to yet assert Critical capability. Standard. 3.4 is weight exfiltration, with listed motives including all the classic instrumentally convergent paths. 3.5 is rogue internal deployments. It’s not clear that these are functionally being treated as distinct from cyber. Finally there are insider threats, which again comes down to ‘do that other stuff.’ Hugging the Face OpenAI is still trying to clean up its failure to disclose previous misalignment incidents. Jason Kwon testified that on September 1 Altman was unaware of the Australia hack, despite company staff knowing about it weeks prior. Anthropic testified that they would have reported a similar incident. You’re Fired Alex Turner, Amber Scorah and Karl Koch respond in Fortune to the firing of OpenAI safety employees, which I covered on Monday, illustrating why AI companies cannot be allowed to self-police. Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch (Fortune): OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. … We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. … The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction. Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. … To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act. They Are Not Ready To Make a Commitment A reminder, in case anyone ever talks about Anthropic’s RSP ‘commitments’: Garrison Lovely: More people should know that, as of January, California law allows AI companies to bind themselves to the mast, by creating safety plans that they are legally compelled to stick to. Even the “safety” company, Anthropic, doesn’t actually do this, instead publishing two versions of their safety plan, with the weaker one being the legally binding one. Anthropic is committed to the one they submitted. The other one is a statement of intent. That is useful, but highly distinct. Anthropic, however, still talks about its RSP as commitments, as seen here. Oliver Habryka: This is the Anthropic RSP “commitment” police Anthropic still is not allowed to say the words “our RSP commits us to X”. Your RSP does not “commit” you to anything. Last time anyone tried to hold you to your “commitments”, you just changed the “commitments”. Please do not use the word “commitment” with regards to the Anthropic RSP. It is highly misleading language. See also previous discussion here. Oliver Habryka (September 18): If you use the word “commit” you need to be happy with other people using the words “you broke your commitment” when you indeed act in conflict with what you “committed” to. I strongly agree with Oliver Habryka. Either you aren’t committed to something, or you can be said to have broken your commitment if you fail to do it. Pick one. Words of Warning It would be nice. roon (OpenAI): every screen of Claude and ChatGPT response should say somewhere “ceterum censeo we must pace the frontier of global machine intelligence progress” the way the uber app lobbied about taxi cartel protectionism Rob Bensinger: IMO you should bid for a message more like: “Recent ‘rogue AI’ incidents at OpenAI and other companies have genuinely frightened us. We have friends and family; we have children, nieces, and nephews. We believe that the race to build vastly superhuman AI poses a genuine and urgent threat to all of us, and we aren’t sure what to do about it. Unilaterally shuttering OpenAI wouldn’t solve the problem, because other companies would build the same technology in our place. Even a domestic ban would be ineffective, so long as China continues racing. What would be effective is an international moratorium on continued development, enacted by the US and China. If you share these concerns, we encourage you to call your elected representative urgently. [contact link] [Q&A link]” Conclusions Not to Jump To The obvious response to seeing all of this would be to conclude that OpenAI has a uniquely broken safety culture, and perhaps say things like delenda est, and to not be thrilled with Anthropic’s or Google’s situation either. Alas, thinking these situations are uniquely bad would be a mistake. Things are not better elsewhere. If anything, things elsewhere are even worse. You don’t want a live look inside of xAI’s or Meta’s safety efforts and culture, or what you would see from a Chinese lab. It is all broken. items.title: Legendary FPS level designer Richard "Levelord" Gray dies at 68
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.content: Prolific first-person shooter level designer Richard "Levelord" Gray died Monday at the age of 68, based on reports shared on social media by Apogee Entertainment yesterday. He had "dealt with cancer on and off for a while now," according to former colleague Joe Siegler. After studying computer engineering in the '80s and tinkering on some early games in COBOL, Gray broke into the industry at the age of 35 in 1994 with the launch of GrayDoom, a set of four maps for the then-new Doom that were widely shared on CompuServe and beyond. The work attracted the attention of Q Studios' Nick Newhard, who contracted Gray to work on level design for the late '90s cult classic Blood. Gray was subsequently hired by 3D Realms, where he said he was given free rein in designing "half the levels" for Duke Nukem 3D. There, he was also responsible for the famous, signed "You're Not Supposed to Be Here" easter egg, which players could find only by using cheats to explore outside of the usual confines of the map. items.title: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
items.author: Justine Calma
items.content: Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning. items.title: Uber’s AI infra, from the inside
items.author: Gergely Orosz
items.content: Stream the latest episode Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The turbopuffer engineering team is doing something really cool: they are completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles to make search faster, cheaper, and more reliable at scale. And they’re documenting all of it! Follow along their rewrite at turbopuffer.com/v3 • Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature to review PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It even supports stacked PRs. Check it out • WorkOS – how do you deal with agents and permissions? WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent and your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human for approval. Works with Claude Code, Codex and MCP gateways. Give it a spin In this episode What do developer tools look like inside Uber, today? They are very different from what you would see at most places. For example, can you guess what service a system called DevPods, Code Inbox, Slate or Wisdom would be providing to engineers? DevPods, Code Inbox, Slate and Wisdom: four of the 20+ internal tools Uber engineers use,day-to-day Today’s episode is a deepdive into the day-to-day tools of devs at Uber, our tour guide being on of Uber’s longest-tenured engineers: Uday Kiran Medisetty. Uday is one of the few Distinguished Engineers at the company, and leads much of the work on agentic AI, today. With Uday, we talk through how Uber’s developer infrastructure prepared it for AI agents. We look at the systems Uber built before generative AI and the new tools that connect agents to its code, internal services, and engineering knowledge. Uday explains how engineers use background agents, why tools like Slate make development (and bugfixing!) more efficient, and how code review is changing. We also cover Uber’s approach to token costs and how it measures productivity as the engineer’s role changes. Takeaways from the conversation with Uday Here are 11 interesting learnings from today’s episode: 1. Uber’s service count changed erratically: in 2015, when Uday joined, there were two services in total. By 2019, there were thousands. In 2026, there will be about the same number of services than in 2019, even though the business is about 10x larger than back then! 2. Uber built most services in-house because off-the-shelf software could not handle its scale – or simply did not exist! Examples of services Uber built because it had to: uOwn: shows who owns a service or asset. Back in 2015, no such vendor existed. M3DB: Uber was emitting about 500 million metrics per second, with no vendor being able to handle this load, so they built it themselves. Observability company Chronosphere was built on top of the open sourced M3DB, and we previously covered how Uber built its observability platform. Cadence: a durable workflow engine for multi-day flows like driver onboarding. No such system existed at the time when Uber needed it. Temporal was built on top of the open sourced Cadence framework. Morpheus: a system combining feature flags and experimentation, including switchback tests, with support for two- and three-sided marketplaces that Uber operates. Again, no such solution existed when Uber needed it. 3. At Uber, cities are a first-class concept that go all the way down to physical infrastructure. Another reason Uber had to build a lot of its custom tooling is how the concept of cities is a “basic primitive” that needs to be handled across systems like observability, feature flagging, deployments, and even service sharding. For example, in the early days, some services had their database sharded by cities. Even today, each city is pinned to a cloud region, and can fall over to another region at any time. We previously covered how Uber moved from bare metal to the cloud. 4. A single AI model gateway has paid lots of dividends. In 2023, Uber’s platform team made the decision that everything built with AI needs to be model- and harness-agnostic. They built Model Gateway to support switching between Anthropic, OpenAI, other vendor models, and now also supports open models they run. Having the Model Gateway in place made it easy to extend with these parts: AI Guard: a middleware run by the security team. It checks all requests and responses, and measures latencies (and flags overly slow models or queries) Spend tracking: spend is tracked per user Visibility: audit logs and session traces 5. AIFX allows engineers to switch harnesses without losing settings. Uber currently supports Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode as harnesses. AIFX (short for AI Foundations) is a wrapper on top of all of these, so when an engineer changes harnesses, all their settings, skills and plugins move with them. 6. Uber has a hybrid approach to AI spend: engineers get allocated a spend tier. When they hit the limit, their manager can sign off to spend more in that month. Basically, for the right type of work, there is no spend limit, but Uber doesn’t want engineers to carelessly burn tokens. A plugin called CostCheck works across sessions and gives tips on how to improve an engineer’s cost profile. Uber has reduced token costs by about 50% the last few months, as we previously covered. 7. All PRs are still reviewed by engineers, but Uber built tools to help devs decide how much time they need to spend on each code change. Uday admits that code review has become a big bottleneck inside the company, and Uber built Code Review to make it easier and more efficient for devs to do these reviews. By the time a dev reviews a change, AI code review has run, screenshots and videos of the feature have been added (when applicable), and risk scores are assigned to the change. 8. Uber had to declare an internal “code red” for its CI system earlier this year. This was because CI jobs more than doubled in a 12-month timeframe, pushing load on CI systems overly high. To keep build speeds at bay, the team moved simple CI jobs (eg linting, build and template rules) to the “inner loop:” so agents run these commands with the afx validate command before opening a PR. 9. Uber tags PRs by the type of work each of those PRs do. In the past, Uber measured “PR velocity:” how long it took for a PR (or, as Uber calls it: a “diff”) to get to production. With agents, doing so makes less sense, because it’s easy to create dozens or even hundreds of PRs, and many of those PRs might have no business impact on the product. So Uber now tags all PRs by type: feature, bugfix, maintenance, testing, or docs. They are seeing the percentage of “feature PRs” going up, and the percentage of “maintenance PRs” going down. I find this categorization to be a clever approach! 10. The job of a software engineer inside a place like Uber is to build context. As Uday reflects on how the job has changed: “The job of engineering is, in some sense: ‘how do you build the right context for the agents to produce reliable output?’ You need to get really good at context engineering. Also, [being good at] multitasking has become a thing. Before, it would take so much time to create a PR, so you would be laser-focused on it. But now you’re constantly switching between so many things. You need to be able to verify your work and pick any code smells from the agent [to avoid] shipping regressions into production. Context engineering, ability to multitask, and ability to review and verify the outputs: these skills have become much more important now because you’re able to parallelize a lot more than before.” 11. Uber’s AI tooling was seemingly built in a year: in reality, it was built on top of a decade worth of dev tooling investment. Minion – built in 2025 – is powered by DevPods, which Uber created in 2017. Uber’s MCP Gateway was fast to build, thanks to existing Thrift and Protobuf registries. Jaeger tracing made Slate routing and Context graph easier, and so on. In Uday’s words: “All the things that we built to make life easier for engineers: it makes it easier for our agents as well!” The Pragmatic Engineer deepdives relevant for this episode • How Uber uses AI for development: inside look • Scaling Uber with Thuan Pham (Uber’s first CTO) • Inside Uber’s move to the Cloud • The Platform and Program Split at Uber • Hypergrowth startups: Uber and CloudKitchens with Charles-Axel Dein • How Uber Built its Observability Platform • How Uber is Measuring Engineering Productivity • Developer Experience at Uber with Gautam Korlam Timestamps 00:00 Intro 02:48 Uday’s early days at Uber 05:40 Uber’s move to microservices 07:55 Uber’s engineering team, then and now 09:05 Developer tooling before AI 16:03 DevPods 19:28 Building for AI agents 29:27 MCP gateway 34:37 Agent Skills repo 38:46 The context graph and Cortana 47:54 PRD and ERD tool 50:45 Minion 54:46 Testing and code review with Bazel, Slate, and Capri 1:12:26 Edge Gateway, Shepherd, and Wisdom 1:21:33 The changing role of engineer and measuring productivity 1:30:40 Uday’s favorite new products References Where to find Uday Kiran Medisetty: • X: https://x.com/udaykiran • LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/udaykiran Mentions during the episode: • Scaling Uber with Thuan Pham (Uber’s first CTO): https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/scaling-uber-with-thuan-pham-ubers • How Uber uses AI for development: inside look: https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/how-uber-uses-ai-for-development • Bazel: https://opensource.google/projects/bazel • Developer Experience at Uber with Gautam Korlam: https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/developer-experience-at-uber • Hypergrowth startups: Uber and CloudKitchens with Charles-Axel Dein: https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/high-growth-startups-uber-and-cloudkitchens • Instinct: https://instinct.com • Muse: https://ai.meta.com/muse • Grok Bot: https://x.ai/bot — Production and marketing by Pen Name.

items.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
items.author: John Timmer
items.content: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. Cutting proteins The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.) items.content: It’s like a big Apple Watch for the home. | Image: Apple Apple only just announced on Tuesday that its first smart display, the HomeView, will arrive on November 13th, but you can already save a couple bucks on it. Right now, you can buy the display for $289.99 ($10 off) in gray and the creamy white “starlight” colorway at Amazon. Sure, it’s a small discount, but deals on new Apple devices ahead of launch are rare. Apple HomeView Where to Buy: $299 $289.99 at Amazon $299 at Apple $299 at Best Buy Expect a full review of the HomeView in November, but my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy spent some brief time with it and likened it to an “iPhone for your home” that looks a bit like an oversized Apple Watch. It features a gorgeous seven-inch square touchscreen that can recognize up to six household members and automatically switch between personalized experiences, displaying information relevant to whoever is using it. As you might already know, the HomeView also doubles as a smart home hub, with support for Matter and Thread. You can use it to control compatible smart home devices, view live feeds and recorded footage from HomeKit Secure Video cameras, and more. It also features a 12-megapixel FaceTime camera for video calls, and doubles as an entertainment device, letting you play music, display photos, and more. Apple’s AI-powered Siri assistant is another big part of the experience, allowing you to ask questions and get information using personal context from your messages, calendar, and emails. That means you can ask it to find your lost keys, play a song someone texted you, pull up a recipe with step-by-step instructions and built-in timers, or help you keep track of your schedule without having to reach for your phone. Read our hands-on impressions.

items.title: Greta Gerwig channels Bowie in psychedelic The Magician's Nephew trailer
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.content: Director Greta Gerwig could have made pretty much any movie she wanted after 2023's Barbie racked up nearly $1.5 billion at the box office. She chose to make Narnia: The Magician's Nephew for Netflix, an adaptation of C.S. Lewis' sixth novel in The Chronicles of Narnia series. Gerwig has said little publicly about the film, other than she was inspired by 1960s-era David Bowie, although she said it would not be a musical. Netflix just released the trailer, set to "Stairway to Heaven," and it's quite the wild psychedelic ride. The first book in the series, The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe, was published in 1950, and Lewis did not initially intend to write any more Narnia adventures. But then an acquaintance asked how the London lamppost ended up in the middle of Narnia's woodland, and Lewis was intrigued enough by the question to start a prequel, The Magician's Nephew, in order to find an answer. Lewis found it difficult to finish the book, however, writing four other Narnia books first before completing The Magician's Nephew in 1955. There have been several adaptations, in various media, of The Chronicles of Narnia, most recently the early 2000s film franchise adapting the first three novels in the series. Those films showed diminishing returns, however, and by 2011 the film rights had expired. There were initial plans to adapt the fourth novel, The Silver Chair. Read full article Comments

items.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers
items.author: Taylor Cuilty
items.content: Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away. Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page. The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people. But returning less data didn’t actually make the query any cheaper. Now maintainers have a direct way to get the curve: we built an endpoint that returns up to 30 weeks of daily star counts in a single request, with no identities attached. Keeping that cheap to serve meant reducing how much data the database processed, not just how much it returned, and the endpoint does that by filtering stars by time before it counts anything. What maintainers need from star history We first addressed the immediate risks to developers and to our database by restricting stargazer and watcher lists to repository administrators and collaborators. After the access change, callers without the required permission could receive an empty response or a 403 Forbidden response. That change also cut off tools that had used the old response to calculate star history, often without displaying or otherwise using the usernames it returned. So we talked with maintainers and tool builders to understand what they still needed. They used star history as an approximate signal of interest: to compare activity before and after a release, or to see whether an announcement reached new developers. What they cared about was the curve. The old API response had made identity look like part of that contract because every timestamp arrived attached to a user. In practice, tools such as Star History needed counts and dates, not usernames or other user data. Once identity was no longer part of the requirement, we could design an aggregate endpoint for the actual job: retrieving changes in star counts over time at a useful resolution. When the API change disrupted Star History, users rallied around the project. GitHub’s Community team listened and connected us with product engineering, who dug into our use case and worked alongside us to design a purpose-built endpoint. A difficult situation became a constructive collaboration between GitHub, Star History, and the broader community—ultimately leading to a better solution. Tianzhou Chen, star-history.com maintainer and Bytebase co-founder Why the original endpoint was expensive Once we knew what maintainers needed, the next step was understanding why the original design couldn’t provide it cheaply. The original GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stargazers endpoint was built to answer a simple question: who starred this repository? It returned a paginated list of people, and if the request specified a custom media type, each entry also included when the star was created. The star model was built for the same job. It records the current set of people who have starred a repository, which keeps showing a star count or a list of stargazers simple. It was not designed as a historical event log: when someone removes a star, that record is removed. When tools began using the list as a time series, reconstructing a growth curve meant retrieving individual identities and processing every current star. Because each page held at most 100 people, the work grew with the repository’s popularity: building the full curve for react/react, with about 251,000 stars, took about 2,511 requests, so tools often ran into rate limits or sampled pages instead of reading them all. Serving a page required the database to query the repository’s current stars. Due to a bug in the pagination implementation, every request also counted all of those stars to work out how many pages existed, even though the caller received only one page of up to 100 people. On a highly starred repository, that meant counting many thousands of entries on every request. In the week before we restricted access, nearly 37,000 of these count queries ran slowly enough to be logged, averaging nearly 3 seconds each, and database safeguards killed more than 1,000 of them, which contributed to request timeouts. The chart below shows what all that counting cost. After we restricted access, the database served about 60% fewer stargazer requests, and the total time it spent on the count query fell by about 80%. Approaches we considered Removing identities handled the privacy requirement. The harder part was keeping each request from scanning the repository’s entire current star set. Keeping events without identities Our first spike kept one record per star and returned the starred_at value without the stargazer’s identity for callers who lacked collaborator access. At first, this looked like the quickest path forward, because it directly served the request we had heard from tool builders. It also closed the identity-harvesting path with a relatively small change to the existing serialization and authorization flow. This approach addressed identity exposure and would have allowed existing tools to keep working. But API consumers would still have to paginate through and process potentially many thousands of individual records to build an aggregate history. It also tied the new use case to an endpoint and pagination model designed for listing people rather than retrieving trends. Aggregating, then paginating Aggregation seemed like the obvious next step. Instead of returning one row per star, the query could group stars into daily or weekly buckets, sort those buckets, and paginate the much smaller result. The problem was where pagination happened. In a straightforward SQL query, the database first finds all stars for the repository, groups them into buckets, and sorts those buckets. Only then does it apply LIMIT, which controls how many buckets are returned, and OFFSET, which determines where the page begins: all matching stars -> bucket every row by day or week -> sort every bucket -> OFFSET/LIMIT -> response For a popular repository, an anonymous request could still scan and aggregate many thousands of index entries to return a handful of buckets. Returning fewer buckets would shrink the JSON response, but it would not reduce the expensive grouping and sorting the database had already performed. For react/react, reading the full history that way would have meant examining roughly 6 million rows, because every one of the 24 requests would have reprocessed all of its stars. To reduce the query cost, we had to narrow the rows before aggregation began. Filtering by time before grouping The design we shipped paginates star history by calendar week. For each request, it translates page and per_page into an indexed created_at range, filters the stars to those weeks, and then groups the matching records into daily counts. A response includes up to 30 weeks, and increasing page moves backward through the repository’s history. indexed date range -> group rows in that range -> daily buckets -> response With the date range applied first, each request processes the weeks being returned instead of every current star in the repository. For tools, that means one request now covers up to 30 weeks of history, no matter how many stars the repository has. For react/react, that’s about 24 requests instead of about 2,511, and the database examines each star about once (roughly 251,000 rows) across the full history. This fits the primary use case because maintainers usually inspect growth across weeks or around a known release, launch, or event. Week-based ranges also align with other repository activity APIs: the response follows the same shape as the weekly commit activity endpoint, GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stats/commit_activity. The time-range design limits each request to a defined period, but it does not limit the number of stars within that range. A week with an unusually large number of stars can therefore still produce a slow or expensive query. The normal request path no longer queries every current star, but exceptionally dense weeks remain a scaling limitation. Comparing the performance of the old and new API paths also surfaced other places where GitHub was counting stars on demand. We found the same pattern on the repository stargazers page on GitHub.com and updated it to use the repository’s cached star count. Slow queries from that page, which had numbered in the hundreds each week, dropped to zero. We recently shipped a similar fix to other stargazer API endpoints. The chart below shows slow and killed stargazer count queries each week, by where they came from. What we learned A smaller response does not always mean a cheaper query. LIMIT and OFFSET reduced the number of results returned, but they did not reduce the grouping and sorting the database had already done. We had to look at the order in which the work happened. Start with what people are actually trying to do. Maintainers needed to compare trends. A list of identities was simply how the old endpoint happened to provide the underlying data. Return only what the use case needs. Anything more is data someone else can misuse. Once we understood the job, we could remove individual identities without taking away the information maintainers relied on. Be clear about the tradeoffs that remain. The new endpoint is safer and more predictable, but calendar boundaries, removed stars, and unusually dense weeks still affect what it can return. Those details are part of the API contract too. Restricting the original endpoint addressed the immediate problem. Listening to maintainers gave us something better than what we started with: star history that’s easier to get, cheaper to serve, and safer for everyone who stars a project. Get repository star history, then share feedback in the GitHub Community discussion. items.title: Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel
items.author: Daniel Abib
items.content: Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI. Why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill. Storage for every application S3 general purpose buckets: Store virtually unlimited objects, including files, images, videos, and documents, for data lakes, cloud-native applications, and mobile apps. S3 delivers the most durable storage in the cloud, designed to provide 99.999999999% (11 nines) data durability and 99.99% availability by default. S3 Tables: Fully managed Apache Iceberg storage optimized for analytics with automated table maintenance and compaction. S3 Tables are directly queryable from any Iceberg REST catalog API-compatible engine, including DuckDB. S3 Vectors: Purpose-built vector storage and query for AI applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search, reducing the cost of uploading, storing, and querying vectors by up to 90%. Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace. Getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds. Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name. Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI: vercel link vercel env pull .env.local The integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere. Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket: import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3"; import { awsCredentialsProvider } from "@vercel/functions/oidc"; const s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION, credentials: awsCredentialsProvider({ roleArn: process.env.AWS_ROLE_ARN, }), }); export async function POST(request) { const formData = await request.formData(); const file = formData.get("file"); await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({ Bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET_NAME, Key: file.name, Body: Buffer.from(await file.arrayBuffer()), ContentType: file.type, })); return Response.json({ success: true }); } Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects. Analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query: import { DuckDBInstance } from "@duckdb/node-api"; import { awsCredentialsProvider } from "@vercel/functions/oidc"; const creds = await awsCredentialsProvider({ roleArn: process.env.AWS_ROLE_ARN, })(); const db = await DuckDBInstance.create(); const conn = await db.connect(); await conn.run("INSTALL aws; LOAD aws; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs; INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;"); await conn.run(` CREATE SECRET s3cred ( TYPE s3, KEY_ID '${creds.accessKeyId}', SECRET '${creds.secretAccessKey}', SESSION_TOKEN '${creds.sessionToken}', REGION '${process.env.AWS_REGION}' ); `); await conn.run(` ATTACH '${process.env.AWS_RESOURCE_ARN}' AS s3tables ( TYPE iceberg, ENDPOINT_TYPE s3_tables ); `); const rows = await (await conn.run(` SELECT town_city, AVG(median_price) AS avg_price FROM s3tables."${process.env.S3_TABLES_NAMESPACE}".town_monthly GROUP BY town_city ORDER BY avg_price DESC LIMIT 10 `)).getRowObjects(); If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled. Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches: import { S3VectorsClient, QueryVectorsCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3vectors"; import { awsCredentialsProvider } from "@vercel/functions/oidc"; const vectors = new S3VectorsClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION, credentials: awsCredentialsProvider({ roleArn: process.env.AWS_ROLE_ARN, }), }); export async function POST(request) { const { embedding } = await request.json(); const result = await vectors.send(new QueryVectorsCommand({ vectorBucketName: process.env.S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME, indexName: "documents", queryVector: { float32: embedding }, topK: 5, returnMetadata: true, })); return Response.json({ matches: result.vectors }); } Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code. Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel. Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval. Using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage. Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace. Join the conversation If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Share your feedback on AWS re:Post for Amazon S3. — Daniel
